entries.1bd9c5dfc2adb69287c8f77ac1fb74634eb79b82: <div sID="gen5639" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="1Sam.18" sID="1Sam.18"/> <div eID="gen5639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5640" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5641" type="x-p"/> In the course of the foregoing chapter we left David in triumph; now in this chapter we have, I. The improvement of his triumphs; he soon became, 1. Saul's constant attendant, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. Jonathan's covenant friend, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.4">4</reference>. 3. The darling of his country, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.16">16</reference>. II. The allays of his triumphs. This is the vanity that accompanies even a right work, that "for it a man is envied," <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">Eccl. iv. 4</reference>. So David was by Saul. 1. He hated him, and sought to kill him himself, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.8-1Sam.18.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 2. He feared him, and contrived how he might have some mischief done him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.12-1Sam.18.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. He proposed to marry his daughter to him; but, [1.] cheated him of the eldest to provoke him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.19">ver. 19</reference>), and, [2.] Gave him the younger, upon conditions which would endanger his life, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.20-1Sam.18.25">ver. 20-25</reference>. But David performed his conditions bravely (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26-1Sam.18.27">ver. 26, 27</reference>), and grew to be more and more esteemed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.28-1Sam.18.30">ver. 28-30</reference>. Still David is rising, but (as all that aim at the crown of life must expect) he had a great deal of difficulty and opposition to grapple with.
entries.83e391ea5350fc90d1784e09b86a96a3913f220a: <div eID="gen5641" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5640" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonathan's Love to David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5642" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father's house. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David went out whithersoever Saul sent him, <hi type="italic">and</hi> behaved himself wisely: and Saul set him over the men of war, and he was accepted in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul's servants. <div eID="gen5642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5643" type="x-p"/> David was anointed to the crown to take it out of Saul's hand, and over Jonathan's head, and yet here we find, <div eID="gen5643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5644" type="x-p"/> I. That Saul, who was now in possession of the crown, reposed a confidence in him, God so ordering it, that he might by his preferment at court be prepared for future service. Saul now took David home with him, and would not suffer him to return again to his retirement, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">v. 2</reference>. And David having signalized himself above the men of war, in taking up the challenge which they declined, <hi type="italic">Saul set him over the men of war</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">v. 5</reference>), not that he made him general (Abner was in that post), but perhaps captain of the life-guard; or, though he was youngest, he ordered him to have the precedency, in recompence of his great services. He employed him in the affairs of government; <hi type="italic">and David went out whithersoever Saul sent him,</hi> showing himself as dutiful as he was bold and courageous. Those that hope to rule must first learn to obey. He had approved himself a dutiful son to Jesse his father, and now a dutiful servant to Saul his master; those that are good in one relation it is to be hoped will be so in another. <div eID="gen5644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5645" type="x-p"/> II. That Jonathan, who was heir to the crown, entered into covenant with him, God so ordering it, that David's way might be the clearer when his rival was his friend. 1. Jonathan conceived an extraordinary kindness and affection for him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he had made an end of speaking to Saul</hi> he fell perfectly in love with him. Whether it refers to his conference with Saul before the battle (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34">ch. xvii. 34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.37">37</reference>), or to that after (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.51">v. 51</reference>), in which it is probable much more was said than is there set down, is uncertain. But, in both, David expressed himself with so much prudence, modesty, and piety, such a felicity of expression, with so much boldness and yet so much sweetness, and all this so natural and unaffected, and the more surprising because of the disadvantages of his education and appearance, <hi type="italic">that the soul of Jonathan was</hi> immediately <hi type="italic">knit</hi> unto <hi type="italic">the soul of David.</hi> Jonathan had formerly set upon a Philistine army with the same faith and bravery with which David had now attacked a Philistine giant; so that there was between them a very near resemblance of affections, dispositions, and counsels, which made their spirits unite so easily, so quickly, so closely, that they seemed but as one soul in two bodies. None had so much reason to dislike David as Jonathan had, because he was to put him by the crown, yet none regards him more. Those that are governed in their love by principles of wisdom and grace will not suffer their affections to be alienated by any secular regards or considerations: the greater thoughts will swallow up and overrule the less. 2. He testified his love to David by a generous present he made him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.4">v. 4</reference>. He was uneasy at seeing so great a soul, though lodged in so fair a body, yet disguised in the mean and despicable dress of a poor shepherd, and therefore takes care to put him speedily into the habit of a courtier (for he gave him a robe) and of a soldier, for he gave him, instead of his staff and sling, a sword and bow, and, instead of his shepherd's scrip, a girdle, either a belt or a sash; and, which made the present much more obliging, they were the same that he himself had worn, and (as a presage of what would follow) he stripped himself of them to dress David in them. Saul's would not fit him, but Jonathan's did. Their bodies were of a size, a circumstance which well agreed with the suitableness of their minds. When Saul put these marks of honour on David he put them off again, because he would first earn them and then wear them; but, now that he had given proofs of the spirit of a prince and a soldier, he was not ashamed to wear the habits of a prince and a soldier. David is seen in Jonathan's clothes, that all may take notice he is a Jonathan's second self. Our Lord Jesus has thus shown his love to us, that he stripped himself to clothe us, emptied himself to enrich us; nay, he did more than Jonathan, he clothed himself with our rags, whereas Jonathan did not put on David's. 3. He endeavored to perpetuate this friendship. So entirely satisfied were they in each other, even at the first interview, that they made a covenant with each other, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.3">v. 3</reference>. Their mutual affection was sincere; and he that bears an honest mind startles not at assurances. True love desires to be constant. Those who love Christ as their own souls will be willing to join themselves to him in an everlasting covenant. <div eID="gen5645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5646" type="x-p"/> III. That both court and country agree to bless him. It is but seldom that they agree in their favourites; yet David was <hi type="italic">accepted in the sight of all the people, and also</hi> (which was strange) <hi type="italic">in the sight of Saul's servants,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">v. 5</reference>. The former cordially loved him, the latter could not for shame but caress and compliment him. And it was certainly a great instance of the power of God's grace in David that he was able to bear all this respect and honour flowing in upon him on a sudden without being lifted up above measure. Those that climb so fast have need of good heads and good hearts. It is more difficult to know how to abound than how to be abased.
entries.c1e490e7896712cf16e56268fe8e576786033f69: <div eID="gen5646" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Honoured by the People; Saul Troubled with an Evil Spirit. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1060.)</title> <div sID="gen5647" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass as they came, when David was returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, that the women came out of all cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul, with tabrets, with joy, and with instruments of music. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the women answered <hi type="italic">one another</hi> as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him; and he said, They have ascribed unto David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed <hi type="italic">but</hi> thousands: and <hi type="italic">what</hi> can he have more but the kingdom? <hi type="super">9</hi> And Saul eyed David from that day and forward. <hi type="super">10</hi> And it came to pass on the morrow, that the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house: and David played with his hand, as at other times: and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a javelin in Saul's hand. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall <hi type="italic">with it.</hi> And David avoided out of his presence twice. <div eID="gen5647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5648" type="x-p"/> Now begin David's troubles, and they not only tread on the heels of his triumphs, but take rise from them, such is the vanity of that in this world which seems greatest. <div eID="gen5648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5649" type="x-p"/> I. He was too much magnified by the common people. Some time after the victory Saul went a triumphant progress through the cities of Israel that lay next him, to receive the congratulations of the country. And, when he made his public entry into any place, the women were most forward to show him respect, as was usual then in public triumphs (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">v. 6</reference>), and they had got a song, it seems, which they sang in their dances (made by some poet or other, that was a great admirer of David's bravery, and was more just than wise, in giving his achievements in the late action the preference before Saul's), the burden of which was, <hi type="italic">Saul had slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.</hi> Such a difference as this Moses made between the numbers of Ephraim and Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">Deut. xxxiii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen5649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5650" type="x-p"/> II. This mightily displeased Saul, and made him envy David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.8-1Sam.18.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. He ought to have considered that they referred only to this late action, and intended not to diminish any of Saul's former exploits; and that in the action now celebrated it was undeniably true that David, in killing Goliath, did in effect slay all the Philistines that were slain that day and defeated the whole army; so that they did but give David his due. It may be, he that composed the song only used a poetic liberty, and intended not any invidious comparison between Saul and David; or, if he did, it was below the great mind of a prince to take notice of such a reflection upon his personal honour, when it appeared that the glory of the public was sincerely intended. But Saul was very wroth, and presently suspected some treasonable design at the bottom of it: <hi type="italic">What can he have more but the kingdom?</hi> This made him eye David as one he was jealous of and sought advantages against (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">v. 9</reference>): his countenance was not towards him as it had been. Proud men cannot endure to hear any praised but themselves, and think all their honour lost that goes by themselves. It is a sign that the Spirit of God has departed from men if they be peevish in their resentment of affronts, envious and suspicious of all about them, and ill-natured in their conduct; for the wisdom from above makes us quite otherwise. <div eID="gen5650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5651" type="x-p"/> III. In his fury he aimed to kill David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10-1Sam.18.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Jealousy is the rage of a man;</hi> it made Saul outrageous against David and impatient to get him out of the way. 1. His fits of frenzy returned upon him. The very next day after he conceived malice against David the evil spirit from God, that had formerly haunted him, seized him again. Those that indulge themselves in envy and uncharitableness <hi type="italic">give place to the devil,</hi> and prepare for the re-entry of the unclean spirit, with seven others more wicked. Where envy is there is confusion. Saul pretended a religious ecstasy: <hi type="italic">He prophesied in the midst of the house,</hi> that is, he had the gestures and motions of a prophet, and humoured the thing well enough to decoy David into a snare, and that he might be fearless of any danger and off his guard; and perhaps designing, if he could but kill him, to impute it to a divine impulse and to charge it upon the spirit of prophecy with which he seemed to be animated: but really it was a hellish fury that actuated him. 2. David, though advanced to a much higher post of honour, disdained not, for his master's service, to return to his harp: <hi type="italic">He played with his hand as at other times.</hi> Let not the highest think any thing below them whereby they may do good and be serviceable to those they are obliged to. 3. He took this opportunity to aim at the death of David. A sword in a madman's hand is a dangerous thing, especially such a madman as Saul was, that was mad with malice. Yet he had a javelin or dart in his hand, which he projected, endeavouring thereby to slay David, not in a sudden passion, but deliberately: <hi type="italic">I will smite David to the wall with it,</hi> with such a desperate force did he throw it. Justly does David complain of his enemies that they hated him with <hi type="italic">a cruel hatred,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.19">Ps. xxv. 19</reference>. No life is thought too precious to be sacrificed to malice. If a grateful sense of the great service David had done to the public could not assuage Saul's fury, yet one would think he should have allowed himself to consider the kindness David was now doing him, in relieving him, as no one else could, against the worst of troubles. Those are possessed with a devilish spirit indeed that render evil for good. Compare David, with his harp in his hand, aiming to serve Saul, and Saul, with his javelin in his hand, aiming to slay David; and observe the meekness and usefulness of God's persecuted people and the brutishness and barbarity of their persecutors. <hi type="italic">The bloodthirsty hate the upright, but the just seek his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Prov. xxix. 10</reference>. 4. David happily avoided the blow twice (namely, now, and afterwards, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.10">ch. xix. 10</reference>); he did not throw the javelin at Saul again, but withdrew, not fighting but flying for his own preservation; though he had both strength and courage enough, and colour of right, to make resistance and revenge the injury, yet he did no more than secure himself, by getting out of the way of it. David, no doubt, had a watchful eye upon Saul's hand, and the javelin in it, and did as bravely in running from it as he did lately in running upon Goliath. Yet his safety must be ascribed to the watchful eye of God's providence upon him, saving his servant from the hurtful sword; and by this narrow escape it seemed he was designed for something extraordinary.
entries.1da80543f6154fdaf6dba49b709ab03fe464bd03: <div eID="gen5651" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Marries Saul's Daughter; Saul's Jealousy of David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1059.)</title> <div sID="gen5652" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And Saul was afraid of David, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was with him, and was departed from Saul. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore Saul removed him from him, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him. <hi type="super">15</hi> Wherefore when Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he was afraid of him. <hi type="super">16</hi> But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he went out and came in before them. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him. <hi type="super">18</hi> And David said unto Saul, Who <hi type="italic">am</hi> I? and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> my life, <hi type="italic">or</hi> my father's family in Israel, that I should be son in law to the king? <hi type="super">19</hi> But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Michal Saul's daughter loved David: and they told Saul, and the thing pleased him. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Saul said, I will give him her, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him. Wherefore Saul said to David, Thou shalt this day be my son in law in <hi type="italic">the one of</hi> the twain. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Saul commanded his servants, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Commune with David secretly, and say, Behold, the king hath delight in thee, and all his servants love thee: now therefore be the king's son in law. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Saul's servants spake those words in the ears of David. And David said, Seemeth it to you <hi type="italic">a</hi> light <hi type="italic">thing</hi> to be a king's son in law, seeing that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a poor man, and lightly esteemed? <hi type="super">24</hi> And the servants of Saul told him, saying, On this manner spake David. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Saul said, Thus shall ye say to David, The king desireth not any dowry, but a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to be avenged of the king's enemies. But Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines. <hi type="super">26</hi> And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son in law: and the days were not expired. <hi type="super">27</hi> Wherefore David arose and went, he and his men, and slew of the Philistines two hundred men; and David brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full tale to the king, that he might be the king's son in law. And Saul gave him Michal his daughter to wife. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Saul saw and knew that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">was</hi> with David, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> Michal Saul's daughter loved him. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Saul was yet the more afraid of David; and Saul became David's enemy continually. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then the princes of the Philistines went forth: and it came to pass, after they went forth, <hi type="italic">that</hi> David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul; so that his name was much set by. <div eID="gen5652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5653" type="x-p"/> Saul had now, in effect, proclaimed war with David. He began in open hostility when he threw the javelin at him. Now we are here told how his enmity proceeded, and how David received the attacks of it. <div eID="gen5653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5654" type="x-p"/> I. See how Saul expressed his malice against David. 1. He was <hi type="italic">afraid of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.12">v. 12</reference>. Perhaps he pretended to be afraid that David would do himself mischief, to force his way to the crown. Those that design ill against others are commonly willing to have it thought that others design ill against them. But David's withdrawal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">v. 11</reference>) was a plain evidence that he was far from such a thought. However, he really stood in awe of him, as Herod feared John, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.20">Mark vi. 20</reference>. Saul was sensible that he had lost the favourable presence of God himself, and that David had it, and for this reason he feared him. Note, Those are truly great and to be reverenced that have God with them. The more <hi type="italic">wisely David behaved himself</hi> the more <hi type="italic">Saul feared him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.15">v. 15</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.29">v. 29</reference>. Men think the way to be feared is to hector and threaten, which makes them feared by fools only, but despised by the wise and good; whereas the way to be both feared and loved, feared by those to whom we would wish to be a terror and loved by those to whom we would wish to be a delight, is to <hi type="italic">behave ourselves wisely.</hi> Wisdom makes the face to shine and commands respect. 2. He removed him from court, and gave him a regiment in the country, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13">v. 13</reference>. He made him captain over 1000, that he might be from under his eye, because he hated the sight of him; and that he might not secure the interest of the courtiers. Yet herein he did impolitely; for it gave David an opportunity of ingratiating himself with the people, who therefore <hi type="italic">loved him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.16">v. 16</reference>) because he <hi type="italic">went out and came in before them,</hi> that is, he presided in the business of his country, civil as well as military, and gave universal satisfaction. 3. He stirred him up to take all occasions of quarrelling with the Philistines and engaging them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17">v. 17</reference>), insinuating to him that hereby he would do good service to his prince (<hi type="italic">be thou valiant for me</hi>), and good service to his God (<hi type="italic">fight the Lord's battles</hi>), and a kindness to himself too, for hereby he would qualify himself for the honour he designed him, which was to marry his eldest daughter to him. This he had merited by killing Goliath, for it was promised by proclamation to him that should do that exploit (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">ch. xvii. 25</reference>); but David was so modest as not to demand it, and now, when Saul proposed it, it was with design of mischief to him, to make him venture upon hazardous attempts, saying in his heart, <hi type="italic">Let the hand of the Philistines be upon him,</hi> hoping that he would some time or other be the death of him; yet how could he expect this when he saw that God was with him? 4. He did what he could to provoke him to discontent and mutiny, by breaking his promise with him, and giving his daughter to another when the time came that she should have been given to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.19">v. 19</reference>. This was as great an affront as he could possibly put upon him, and touched him both in his honour and in his love. He therefore thought David's resentment of it would break out in some indecency or other, in word or deed, which might give him an advantage against him to take him off by the course of law. Thus evil men seek mischief. 5. When he was disappointed in his, he proffered him his other daughter (who it seems had a secret kindness for David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.20">v. 20</reference>), but with this design, that she might be <hi type="italic">a snare to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.21">v. 21</reference>. (1.) Perhaps he hoped that she would, even after her marriage to David, take part with her father against her husband, and give him an opportunity of doing David an unkindness. However, (2.) The conditions of the marriage, he hoped, would be his destruction; for (so zealous will Saul seem against the Philistines) the conditions of the marriage must be that he killed 100 Philistines, and, as proofs that those he had slain were uncircumcised, he must bring in their foreskins cut off; this would be a just reproach upon the Philistines, who hated circumcision as it was an ordinance of God; and perhaps David, in doing this, would the more exasperate them against him, and make them seek to be revenged on him, which was the thing that Saul desired and designed, much more than to be avenged on the Philistines: <hi type="italic">For Saul thought to make David fall by the Philistines,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.25">v. 25</reference>. See here, [1.] What cheats bad men put upon themselves. Saul's conscience would not suffer him, except when the evil spirit was actually upon him, to aim at David's life himself, for even he could not but conceive a horror at the thought of murdering such an innocent and excellent person; but he thought that to expose him designedly to the Philistines had nothing bad in it (<hi type="italic">Let not my hand be upon him, but the hand of the Philistines</hi>), whereas that malicious design against him was as truly murder before God as if he had slain him with his own hands. [2.] What cheats they put upon the world. Saul pretended extraordinary kindness for David even when he aimed at his ruin, and was actually plotting it: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be my son-in-law,</hi> says he (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.21">v. 21</reference>), notwithstanding he hated him implacably. Perhaps David refers to this when (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">Ps. lv. 21</reference>) he speaks of his enemy as one whose words were <hi type="italic">smoother than butter, but war was in his heart.</hi> It is probable that Saul's employing his servants to persuade David to enter into a treaty of a match with his daughter Michal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.22">v. 22</reference>) arose from an apprehension that either his having cheated him about his elder daughter (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.19">v. 19</reference>) or the hardness of the terms he intended now to propose would make him decline it. <div eID="gen5654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5655" type="x-p"/> II. See how David conducted himself when the tide of Saul's displeasure ran thus high against him. <div eID="gen5655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5656" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">He behaved himself wisely in all his ways.</hi> He perceived Saul's jealousy of him, which made him very cautious and circumspect in every thing he said and did, and careful to give no offence. He did not complain of hard measure more make himself the head of a party, but managed all the affairs he was entrusted with as one that made it his business to do real service to his king and country, looking upon that to be the end of his preferment. And then <hi type="italic">the Lord was with him</hi> to give him success in all his undertakings. Though he procured Saul's ill-will by it, yet he obtained God's favour. Compare this with <reference osisRef="Ps.101.2">Ps. ci. 2</reference>, where it is David's promise, <hi type="italic">I will behave myself wisely;</hi> and that promise he here performed; and it is his prayer, <hi type="italic">O, when wilt thou come unto me?</hi> And that prayer God here answered: <hi type="italic">The Lord was with him.</hi> However blind fortune may seem to favour fools, God will own and bless those that behave themselves wisely. <div eID="gen5656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5657" type="x-p"/> 2. When it was proposed to him to be son-in-law to the king he once and again received the proposal with all possible modesty and humility. When Saul proposed his elder daughter to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">v. 18</reference>) he said, <hi type="italic">Who am I, and what is my life?</hi> When the courtier proposed the younger, he took no notice of the affront Saul had put upon him in disposing of the elder from him, but continued in the same mind (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Seemeth it a light thing to you to be a king's son-in-law, seeing that I am a poor man and lightly esteemed?</hi> He knew Michal loved him, and yet did not offer to improve his interest in her affections for the gaining of her without her father's consent, but waited till it was proposed to him. And then see, (1.) How highly he speaks of the honour offered him: <hi type="italic">To be son-in-law to the king.</hi> Though his king was but an upstart, in his original as mean as himself, in his management no better than he should be, yet, being a crowned head, he speaks of him and the royal family with all due respect. Note, Religion is so far from teaching us to be rude and unmannerly that it does not allow us to be so. We must <hi type="italic">render honour to whom honour is due.</hi> (2.) How humbly he speaks of himself: <hi type="italic">Who am I?</hi> This did not proceed from a mean, abject, sneaking spirit, for when there was occasion he made it appear that he had as high a sense of honour as most men; nor was it from his jealousy of Saul (though he had reason enough to fear a snake under the green grass), but from him true and deep humility: <hi type="italic">Who am I, a poor man, and lightly esteemed?</hi> David had as much reason as any man to value himself. He was of an ancient and honourable family of Judah, a comely person, a great statesman and soldier; his achievements were great, for he had won Goliath's head and Michal's heart. He knew himself destined by the divine counsels to the throne of Israel, and yet, <hi type="italic">Whom am I, and what is my life?</hi> Note, It well becomes us, however God has advanced us, always to have low thoughts of ourselves. <hi type="italic">He that humbleth himself shall be exalted.</hi> And, if David thus magnified the honour of being son-in-law to the king, how should we magnify the honour of being sons (not in law, but in gospel) to the King of kings! <hi type="italic">Behold what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us!</hi> Who are we that we should be thus dignified? <div eID="gen5657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5658" type="x-p"/> 3. When the slaying of 100 Philistines was made the condition of David's marrying Saul's daughter he readily closed with it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">It pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law</hi> upon those terms; and, before the time given him for the action had expired, he doubled the demand, and slew 200, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.27">v. 27</reference>. He would not seem to suspect that Saul designed his hurt by it (though he had reason enough), but would rather act as if Saul had meant to consult his honour, and therefore cheerfully undertook it, as became a brave soldier and a true lover, though we may suppose it uneasy to Michal. David hereby discovered likewise, (1.) A great confidence in the divine protection. He knew God was with him, and therefore, whatever Saul hoped, David did not fear falling by the Philistines, though he must needs expose himself much by such an undertaking as this. (2.) A great zeal for the good of his country, which he would not decline any occasion of doing service to, though with the hazard of his life. (3.) A right notion of honour, which consists not so much in being preferred as in deserving to be so. David was then pleased with the thoughts of being the king's son-in-law when he found the honour set at this high price, being more solicitous how to merit it than how to obtain it; nor could he wear it with satisfaction till he had won it. <div eID="gen5658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5659" type="x-p"/> 4. Even after he was married he continued his good services to Israel. When the princes of the Philistines began to move towards another war David was ready to oppose them, and <hi type="italic">behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.30">v. 30</reference>. The law dispensed with men from going to war the first year after they were married (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.5">Deut. xxiv. 5</reference>), but David loved his country too well to make use of that dispensation. Many that have shown themselves forward to serve the public when they have been in pursuit of preferment have declined it when they have gained their point; but David acted from more generous principles. <div eID="gen5659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5660" type="x-p"/> III. Observe how God brought good to David out of Saul's project against him. 1. Saul gave him his daughter to be a snare to him, but in this respect that marriage was a kindness to him, that his being Saul's son-in-law made his succeeding him much the less invidious, especially when so many of his sons were slain with him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">ch. xxxi. 2</reference>. 2. Saul thought, by putting him upon dangerous services, to have him taken off, but that very thing confirmed his interest in the people; for the more he did against the Philistines the better they loved him, so that <hi type="italic">his name was much set by</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.30">v. 30</reference>), which would make his coming to the crown the more easy. Thus God makes even the wrath of man to praise him and serves his designs of kindness to his own people by it.  <chapter eID="1Sam.18"/> <div eID="gen5660" type="x-p"/>

entries.7d55468221c51d14b07e7e8f78ccdab9076dcedd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2688"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen3653" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.4">1Sa 18:1-4</reference>. Jonathan Loves David.<div eID="gen3653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2688"/><hi type="bold">1. the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David--</hi>They were nearly of an age. The prince had taken little interest in David as a minstrel; but his heroism and modest, manly bearing, his piety and high endowments, kindled the flame not of admiration only, but of affection, in the congenial mind of Jonathan. <div eID="gen3654" type="x-p"/>
entries.649f5678812fff64672cf33f1bfe08788b924538: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2689"/><div sID="gen3655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2689"/><hi type="bold">2. Saul would let him go no more home--</hi>He was established as a permanent resident at court. <div eID="gen3655" type="x-p"/>
entries.01510c065eff6ca11bc8ffce10a1d499a561e89a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2690"/><div sID="gen3656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2690"/><hi type="bold">3. Then Jonathan and David made a covenant--</hi>Such covenants of brotherhood are frequent in the East. They are ratified by certain ceremonies, and in presence of witnesses, that the persons covenanting will be sworn brothers for life. <div eID="gen3656" type="x-p"/>
entries.c42d588aee9bfdcad455c8774aa829cdcac480e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2691"/><div sID="gen3657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2691"/><hi type="bold">4. Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David--</hi>To receive any part of the dress which had been worn by a sovereign, or his eldest son and heir, is deemed, in the East, the highest honor which can be conferred on a subject (see on <reference osisRef="Esth.6.8">Es 6:8</reference>). The girdle, being connected with the sword and the bow, may be considered as being part of the military dress, and great value is attached to it in the East.<div eID="gen3657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3658" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5-1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:5-9</reference>. Saul Envies His Praise. <div eID="gen3658" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cda1693c5c2e0881ec507079ea2e9c1a953107a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2692"/><div sID="gen3659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2692"/><hi type="bold">6. the women came out of all cities of Israel--</hi>in the homeward march from the pursuit of the Philistines. This is a characteristic trait of Oriental manners. On the return of friends long absent, and particularly on the return of a victorious army, bands of women and children issue from the towns and villages, to form a triumphal procession, to celebrate the victory, and, as they go along, to gratify the soldiers with dancing, instrumental music, and extempore songs, in honor of the generals who have earned the highest distinction by feats of gallantry. The Hebrew women, therefore, were merely paying the customary gratulations to David as the deliverer of their country, but they committed a great indiscretion by praising a subject at the expense of their sovereign. <div eID="gen3659" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a050ae67bad518940361519645aceb4898167e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2693"/><div sID="gen3660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2693"/><hi type="bold">9. Saul eyed David--</hi>that is, invidiously, with secret and malignant hatred.<div eID="gen3660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3661" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10-1Sam.18.12">1Sa 18:10-12</reference>. Seeks to Kill Him. <div eID="gen3661" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf224f9551f8492f374084e397df394b61ddb953: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2694"/><div sID="gen3662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2694"/><hi type="bold">10. on the morrow, that the evil spirit from God came upon Saul--</hi>This rankling thought brought on a sudden paroxysm of his mental malady.<div eID="gen3662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he prophesied--</hi>The term denotes one under the influence either of a good or a bad spirit. In the present it is used to express that Saul was in a frenzy. David, perceiving the symptoms, hastened, by the soothing strains of his harp, to allay the stormy agitation of the royal mind. But before its mollifying influence could be felt, Saul hurled a javelin at the head of the young musician.<div eID="gen3663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there was a javelin in Saul's hand--</hi>Had it been followed by a fatal result, the deed would have been considered the act of an irresponsible maniac. It was repeated more than once ineffectually, and Saul became impressed with a dread of David as under the special protection of Providence.<div eID="gen3664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3665" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13-1Sam.18.16">1Sa 18:13-16</reference>. Fears Him for His Good Success. <div eID="gen3665" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9450aec2a0bc44cc316315c29cae807f2704bfc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2695"/><div sID="gen3666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2695"/><hi type="bold">13. Therefore Saul removed him from him--</hi>sent him away from the court, where the principal persons, including his own son, were spellbound with admiration of the young and pious warrior.<div eID="gen3666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3667" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made him captain over a thousand--</hi>gave him a military commission, which was intended to be an honorable exile. But this post of duty served only to draw out before the public the extraordinary and varied qualities of his character, and to give him a stronger hold of the people's affections.<div eID="gen3667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3668" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.21">1Sa 18:17-21</reference>. He Offers Him His Daughter for a Snare. <div eID="gen3668" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7211750b568609d66166d58fa728c48497fee53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2696"/><div sID="gen3669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2696"/><hi type="bold">17. Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife--</hi>Though bound to this already [1Sa 17:25], he had found it convenient to forget his former promise. He now holds it out as a new offer, which would tempt David to give additional proofs of his valor. But the fickle and perfidious monarch broke his pledge at the time when the marriage was on the eve of being celebrated, and bestowed Merab on another man (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.8">2Sa 21:8</reference>); an indignity as well as a wrong, which was calculated deeply to wound the feelings and provoke the resentment of David. Perhaps it was intended to do so, that advantage might be taken of his indiscretion. But David was preserved from this snare. <div eID="gen3669" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d1987ff1f9758916b3adf91982c048cb836b14a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2697"/><div sID="gen3670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2697"/><hi type="bold">20. Michal Saul's daughter loved David--</hi>This must have happened some time after.<div eID="gen3670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they told Saul, and the thing pleased him--</hi>Not from any favor to David, but he saw that it would be turned to the advancement of his malicious purposes, and the more so when, by the artful intrigues and flattery of his spies, the loyal sentiments of David were discovered. <div eID="gen3671" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae8a412d40dcda49c5d5d0492e492a10f6c4a27a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2698"/><div sID="gen3672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2698"/><hi type="bold">25. The king desireth not any dowry--</hi>In Eastern countries the husband purchases his wife either by gifts or services. As neither David nor his family were in circumstances to give a suitable dowry for a princess, the king intimated that he would be graciously pleased to accept some gallant deed in the public service.<div eID="gen3672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a hundred foreskins of the Philistines--</hi>Such mutilations on the bodies of their slain enemies were commonly practised in ancient war, and the number told indicated the glory of the victory. Saul's willingness to accept a public service had an air of liberality, while his choice of so difficult and hazardous a service seemed only putting a proper value on gaining the hand of a king's daughter. But he covered unprincipled malice against David under this proposal, which exhibited a zeal for God and the covenant of circumcision. <div eID="gen3673" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0e58e5dcb868ee3bc56ad4aca9ae41dc6831fc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2699"/><div sID="gen3674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2699"/><hi type="bold">26. the days were not expired--</hi>The period within which this exploit was to be achieved was not exhausted. <div eID="gen3674" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1fd84c8b1d5ada1f906d078f72d55c8cacf64a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2700"/><div sID="gen3675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2700"/><hi type="bold">27. David ... slew of the Philistines two hundred men--</hi>The number was doubled, partly to show his respect and attachment to the princess, and partly to oblige Saul to the fulfilment of his pledge. <div eID="gen3675" type="x-p"/>
entries.c15703b348f605cadf0989567b8795c274089fe5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2701"/><div sID="gen3676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2701"/><hi type="bold">29. Saul was yet the more afraid of David--</hi>because Providence had visibly favored him, by not only defeating the conspiracy against his life, but through his royal alliance paving his way to the throne. <chapter eID="1Sam.18"/>

entries.ede2d97653877fb9572c191f3d0ec1314794449a: <div eID="gen10235" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10236" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10237" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10237" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10236" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10238" type="x-p"/> Jonathan and David commence a lasting friendship; and David acts prudently with respect to Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.5">1Sam 18:1-5</reference>. Saul becomes jealous of David, on account of the esteem in which he is held in Israel; and, in his fury endeavors to destroy him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.12">1Sam 18:6-12</reference>. David is made captain over a thousand; and the people love and respect him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13-1Sam.18.16">1Sam 18:13-16</reference>. Saul, in order to ensnare him, offers him his daughter in marriage, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.24">1Sam 18:17-24</reference>; and requires a hundred foreskins of the Philistines for dowry; hoping that, in endeavoring to procure them, David might fall by the hands of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.25">1Sam 18:25</reference>. David agrees to the conditions, fulfils them, and has Michal to wife, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26-1Sam.18.30">1Sam 18:26-30</reference>. <div eID="gen10238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10239" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> When he had made an end of speaking - These first five verses are omitted by the Septuagint. See the notes on the preceding chapter, 1 Samuel 17 (note). <div eID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10241" type="x-p"/> Jonathan loved him as his own soul - The most intimate friendship subsisted between them; and they loved each other with pure hearts fervently. No love was lost between them; each was worthy of the other. They had a friendship which could not be affected with changes or chances, and which exemplified all that the ancients have said on the subject; Την φιλιαν ισοτητα ειναι, και μιαν ψυχην, τον φιλον ἑτερον αυτον; "Friendship produces an entire sameness; it is one soul in two bodies: a friend is another self."
entries.7a190c70d249a07375c6bffce0287a8a81a4e0d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10242" type="x-p"/> Jonathan stripped himself - Presents of clothes or rich robes, in token of respect and friendship, are frequent in the East. And how frequently arms and clothing were presented by warriors to each other in token of friendship, may be seen in Homer and other ancient writers.
entries.7a87985bf9ddef312d13c1d1be5dc156f4dbbea6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10243" type="x-p"/> Set him over the men of war - Made him generalissimo; or what we would call field marshal.
entries.ae37c372fc353fcbe082bcd18320139815e1bb7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10244" type="x-p"/> When David was returned - This verse connects well with the 54th verse of the preceding chapter; and carries on the narration without any break or interruption. See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.54">1Sam 17:54</reference>. <div eID="gen10244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10245" type="x-p"/> The women came out - It was the principal business of certain women to celebrate victories, sing at funerals, etc. <div eID="gen10245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10246" type="x-p"/> With instruments of music - The original word (שלשים shalishim) signifies instruments with three strings; and is, I think, properly translated by the Vulgate, cum sistris, "with sistrums." This instrument is well known as being used among the ancient Egyptians: it was made of brass, and had three, sometimes more, brass rods across; which, being loose in their holes, made a jingling noise when the instrument was shaken.
entries.fcbf8797a28a6ebf564daf195aaac845d2241f53: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10247" type="x-p"/> Saul hath slain his thousands - As it cannot literally be true that Saul had slain thousands, and David ten thousands; it would be well to translate the passage thus: Saul hath smitten or fought against thousands; David against tens of thousands. "Though Saul has been victorious in all his battles; yet he has not had such great odds against him as David has had; Saul, indeed, has been opposed by thousands; David, by ten thousands." We may here remark that the Philistines had drawn out their whole forces at this time: and when Goliath was slain, they were totally discomfited by the Israelites, led on chiefly by David.
entries.e7131e7a34e62093f777f78980de5c63c85bcfef: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10248" type="x-p"/> The evil spirit from God - See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.14">1Sam 16:14</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen10248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10249" type="x-p"/> He prophesied in the midst of the house - He was beside himself; made prayers, supplications, and incoherent imprecations: "God preserve my life," "Destroy my enemies," or such like prayers, might frequently escape from him in his agitated state. The Arabic intimates that he was actually possessed by an evil spirit, and that through it he uttered a sort of demoniacal predictions. <div eID="gen10249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10250" type="x-p"/> But let us examine the original more closely: it is said that Saul prophesied in the midst of his house, that is, he prayed in his family, while David was playing on the harp; and then suddenly threw his javelin, intending to have killed David. Let it be observed that the word ויתנבא vaiyithnabbe is the third person singular of the future hithpael; the sign of which is not only to do an action on or for one's self, but also to feign or pretend to do it. The meaning seems to be, Saul pretended to be praying in his family, the better to conceal his murderous intentions, and render David unsuspicious; who was, probably, at this time performing the musical part of the family worship. This view of the subject makes the whole case natural and plain.
entries.1360705e067c86ba5b563a99eb199df3e49bbc5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10251" type="x-p"/> Saul cast the javelin - The javelin or spear was the emblem of regal authority; kings always had it at hand, and in ancient monuments they are always represented with it. <div eID="gen10251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10252" type="x-p"/> In ancient times, says Justin, kings used a spear instead of a diadem: Per ea tempora reges hastas pro diademate habebant, Hist. lib. xliii. And as spears were the emblems of supreme power, hence they were reputed as attributes of the Divinity, and were worshipped as representatives of the gods. Ab origne verum, pro Diis immortalibus veteres Hastas coluerent, ob cujus religionis memoriam, adhuc deorum simulachris Hastae adduntur. - Ibid.
entries.28db4c2f031a917811c46a5bb26152f9db401f8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10253" type="x-p"/> Made him his captain - This was under pretense of doing him honor, when it was in effect only to rid himself of the object of his envy.
entries.1974adce4e01243a2867be10669a079f93808796: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10254" type="x-p"/> He was afraid of him - He saw that, by his prudent conduct, he was every day gaining increasing influence.
entries.4e90d8e39fb733b063fea09d22fd2216a9253d32: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10255" type="x-p"/> Fight the Lord's battles - Mr. Calmet properly remarks that the wars of the Hebrews, while conducted by the express orders of God, were truly the wars of the Lord; but when the spirit of worldly ambition and domination became mingled with them, they were no longer the wars of the Lord, but wars of lust and profanity.
entries.bfb8b46fdbe031afdb6338de2d576327f92a6d70: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10256" type="x-p"/> That she may be a snare to him - Saul had already determined the condition on which he would give his daughter to David; viz., that he should slay one hundred Philistines: this he supposed he would undertake for the love of Michal, and that he must necessarily perish in the attempt; and thus Michal would become a snare to him.
entries.b2217b49d13dea5220271a9b758cd5bb891a0641: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10257" type="x-p"/> But a hundred foreskins - That is, Thou shalt slay one hundred Philistines, and thou shalt produce their foreskins, as a proof, not only that thou hast killed one hundred men, but that these are of the uncircumcised. A custom similar to this still prevails among the Abyssinians, according to Bruce. See his Travels.
entries.63de6c6e111ac8b01b3fc5d735fab6af61e6de23: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen10257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10258" type="x-p"/> Slew - two hundred men - The Septuagint has only one hundred men. Saul covenanted with David for a hundred; and David himself says, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.14">2Sam 3:14</reference>, that he espoused Michal for a hundred: hence it is likely that one hundred is the true reading.
entries.3f3b3feae7a8dc576d0d14c687c01342bc5d7cbe: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen10258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10259" type="x-p"/> Then the princes of the Philistines went forth - Probably to avenge themselves on David and the Israelites: but of this war we know no more than that David was more skillful and successful in it than any of the other officers of Saul. His military skill was greater, and his success was proportionate to his skill and courage; hence it is said, he behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul.  <chapter eID="1Sam.18"/> <div eID="gen10259" type="x-p"/>

entries.136280afca1a74203c121646534dd377932cc763: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen3968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3969" type="x-p"/> The bond of friendship which Jonathan formed with David was so evidently the main point, that in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1">1Sa 18:1</reference> the writer commences with the love of Jonathan to David, and then after that proceeds in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> to observe that Saul took David to himself from that day forward; whereas it is very evident that Saul told David, either at the time of his conversation with him or immediately afterwards, that he was henceforth to remain with him, i.e., in his service. “<hi type="italic">The soul of Jonathan bound itself</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. chained itself; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.44.30">Gen 44:30</reference>) <hi type="italic">to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him as his soul</hi>.” The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> ויּאהבו with the suffix ו attached to the imperfect is very rare, and hence the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> ויּאהבהוּ (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §249, <hi type="italic">b</hi>., and Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. p. 469). לשׁוּב, to return to his house, viz., to engage in his former occupation as shepherd.
entries.ea3e0775717efbec51bb3e5be014b946a0767e7f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.3">1Sa 18:3</reference> <div eID="gen3969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3970" type="x-p"/> Jonathan <hi type="italic">made a covenant</hi> (i.e., a covenant of friendship) <hi type="italic">and</hi> (i.e., with) <hi type="italic">David</hi>, because he loved him as his soul.
entries.74a1860b963d93774357fc5c324dca43c83b4c18: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.4">1Sa 18:4</reference> <div eID="gen3970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3971" type="x-p"/> As a sign and pledge of his friendship, Jonathan gave David <hi type="italic">his clothes and his armour</hi>. <hi type="italic">Meil</hi>, the upper coat or cloak. <hi type="italic">Maddim</hi> is probably the <hi type="italic">armour coat</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.39">1Sa 17:39</reference>). This is implied in the word ועד, which is repeated three times, and by which the different arms were attached more closely to מדּיו. For the act itself, compare the exchange of armour made by Glaucus and Diomedes (Hom. <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. vi. 230). This seems to have been a common custom in very ancient times, as we meet with it also among the early Celts (see Macpherson’s <hi type="italic">Ossian</hi>).
entries.284d8cc5aab3765fdfca4317335a5feda9dc2ff5: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> <div eID="gen3971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3972" type="x-p"/> And David <hi type="italic">went out</hi>, sc., to battle; <hi type="italic">whithersoever Saul sent him, he acted wisely and prosperously</hi> (ישׂכּיל, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.1.8">Jos 1:8</reference> : see at <reference osisRef="Deut.29.8">Deu 29:8</reference>). Saul placed him above the men of war in consequence, made him one of their commanders; and he pleased all the people, and the servants of Saul also, i.e., the courtiers of the king, who are envious as a general rule.
entries.a3e4e42f0ee34340b7872cd34355826bcd41b522: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.16">1Sa 18:6-16</reference> <hi type="italic">Saul’s jealousy towards David</hi>.<note placement="foot">The section <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:6-14</reference> is supposed by Thenius and others to have been taken by the compiler from a different source from the previous one, and not to have been written by the same author: (1) because the same thing is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13">1Sa 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:14</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, though in a somewhat altered form, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference> occur again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9-1Sam.19.10">1Sa 19:9-10</reference>, with a few different words, and in a more appropriate connection; (2) because the contents of <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.9">1Sa 19:9</reference>, and the word ממּחרת in <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.10">1Sa 19:10</reference>, are most directly opposed to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and 1Sa 18:5. On these grounds, no doubt, the lxx have not only omitted the beginning of <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference> from their version, but also <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference>-11. But the supposed discrepancy between <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, - viz., that Saul could not have kept David by his side from attachment to him, or have placed him over his men of war after several prosperous expeditions, as is stated in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>, if he had looked upon him with jealous eyes from the very first day, or if his jealousy had broken out on the second day in the way described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.11">1Sa 18:11</reference>, - is founded upon two erroneous assumptions; viz., (1) that the facts contained in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.1-1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:1-5</reference> were contemporaneous with those in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.14">1Sa 18:6-14</reference>; and (2) that everything contained in these two sections is to be regarded as strictly chronological. But the fact recorded in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.2">1Sa 18:2</reference>, namely, that Saul took David to himself, and did not allow him to go back to his father’s house any more, occurred unquestionably some time earlier than those mentioned in 1Sa 18:6. with their consequences. Saul took David to himself immediately after the defeat of Goliath, and before the war had been brought to an end. But the celebration of the victory, in which the paean of the women excited jealousy in Saul’s mind, did not take place till the return of the people and of the king at the close of the war. How long the war lasted we do not know; but from the fact that the Israelites pursued the flying Philistines to Gath and Ekron, and then plundered the camp of the Philistines after that (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.52-1Sam.17.53">1Sa 17:52-53</reference>), it certainly follows that some days, if not weeks, must have elapsed between David’s victory over Goliath and the celebration of the triumph, after the expulsion of the Philistines from the land. Thus far the events described in the two sections are arranged in their chronological order; but for all the rest the facts are arranged antithetically, according to their peculiar character, whilst the consequences, which reached further than the facts that gave rise to them, and were to some extent contemporaneous, are appended immediately to the facts themselves. Thus David’s going out whithersoever Saul sent him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>) may indeed have commenced during the pursuit of the flying Philistines; but it reached far beyond this war, and continued even while Saul was looking upon him with jealous eyes. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> contains a general remark, with which the historian brings to a close one side of the relation between David and Saul, which grew out of David’s victory. He then proceeds in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference> to give the other side, and rounds off this paragraph also (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14-1Sam.18.16">1Sa 18:14-16</reference>) with a general remark, the substance of which resembles, in the main, the substance of 1Sa 18:5. At the same time it implies some progress, inasmuch as the delight of the people at the acts performed by David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference>) grew into love to David itself. This same progress is also apparent in <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.13">1Sa 18:13</reference> (“<hi type="italic">Saul made him captain over a thousand</hi>”), as compared with <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5">1Sa 18:5</reference> (“<hi type="italic">Saul set him over the men of war</hi>”). Whether the elevation of David into a captain over a thousand was a higher promotion than his appointment over the men of war, or the latter expression is to be taken as simply a more general or indefinite term, denoting his promotion to the rank of commander-in-chief, is a point which can hardly be determined with certainty.</note>  - Saul had no sooner attached the conqueror of Goliath to his court, than he began to be jealous of him. The occasion for his jealousy was the celebration of victory at the close of the war with the Philistines.  <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen3972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3973" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When they came</hi>,” i.e., when the warriors returned with Saul from the war, “<hi type="italic">when</hi> (as is added to explain what follows) <hi type="italic">David returned from the slaughter</hi>,” i.e., from the war in which he had slain Goliath, the women came out of all the towns of Israel, “<hi type="italic">to singing and dancing</hi>,” i.e., to celebrate the victory with singing and choral dancing (see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>), “<hi type="italic">to meet king Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with triangles</hi>.” שׂמהה is used here to signify expressions of joy, a <hi type="italic">fête</hi>, as in Jdg 16:23, etc. The striking position in which the word stands, viz., between two musical instruments, shows that, the word is to be understood here as referring specially to songs of rejoicing, since according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:7</reference> their playing was accompanied with singing. The women who “<hi type="italic">sported</hi>” (משׂחקות), i.e., performed mimic dances, sang in alternate choruses (“<hi type="italic">answered</hi>,” as in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.21">Exo 15:21</reference>), “<hi type="italic">Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands</hi>.”
entries.53c9eb80f38974d52a6ee63269127cce7ec34235: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">1Sa 18:18</reference> <div eID="gen3978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3979" type="x-p"/> But David replied with true humility, without suspecting the craftiness of Saul: “<hi type="italic">Who am I, and what is my condition in life, my father’s family in Israel, that I should become son-in-law to the king?</hi>” חיּי מי is a difficult expression, and has been translated in different ways, as the meaning which suggests itself first (viz., “<hi type="italic">what is my life</hi>”) is neither reconcilable with the מי (the interrogative personal pronoun), nor suitable to the context. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 471) and Böttcher give the meaning “<hi type="italic">people</hi>” for חיּים, and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §179, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.) the meaning “<hi type="italic">family</hi>.” But neither of these meanings can be established. חיּים seems evidently to signify the condition in life, the relation in which a person stands to others, and מי is to be explained on the ground that David referred to the persons who formed the class to which he belonged. “<hi type="italic">My father’s family</hi>” includes all his relations. David’s meaning was, that neither on personal grounds, nor on account of his social standing, nor because of his lineage, could he make the slightest pretension to the honour of becoming the son-in-law of the king.
entries.926455e91eed44ff54f0d7ffc4fd47c51c93e455: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.19">1Sa 18:19</reference> <div eID="gen3979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> But Saul did not keep his promise. When the time arrived for its fulfilment, <hi type="italic">he gave his daughter to Adriel the Meholathite</hi>, a man of whom nothing further is known.<note placement="foot"><reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.19">1Sa 18:17-19</reference> are omitted from the Septuagint version; but they are so, no doubt, only because Saul’s first promise was without result so far as David was concerned.</note>
entries.991c47ee9b63de9f8e94147203563c9d9887226f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.20-1Sam.18.21">1Sa 18:20-21</reference> <hi type="italic">Michal is married to David</hi>. - The pretext under which Saul broke his promise is not given, but it appears to have been, at any rate in part, that Merab had no love to David. This may be inferred from <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17">1Sa 18:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">1Sa 18:18</reference>, compared with 1Sa 18:20. <hi type="italic">Michal, the younger daughter of Saul, loved David</hi>. When Saul was told this, the thing was quite right in his eyes. He said, “<hi type="italic">I will give her to him, that she may become a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may come upon him</hi>” (sc., if he tries to get the price which I shall require a dowry; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.25">1Sa 18:25</reference>). He therefore said to David, “<hi type="italic">In a second way</hi> (בּשׁתּים, as in <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job 33:14</reference>) <hi type="italic">shalt thou become my son-in-law</hi>.” Saul said this casually to David; but he made no reply, because he had found out the fickleness of Saul, and therefore put no further trust in his words.
entries.67b82393fb0415341c785cb03c3d110715f2aa8f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.22">1Sa 18:22</reference> <div eID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3981" type="x-p"/> Saul therefore employed his courtiers to persuade David to accept his offer. In this way we may reconcile in a very simple manner the apparent discrepancy, that Saul is said to have offered his daughter to David himself, and yet he commissioned his servants to talk to David privately of the king’s willingness to give him his daughter. The omission of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.18.21">1Sa 18:21</reference></hi> in the Septuagint is to be explained partly from the fact that בּשׁתּים points back to <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17-1Sam.18.19">1Sa 18:17-19</reference>, which are wanting in this version, and partly also in all probability from the idea entertained by the translators that the statement itself is at variance with 1Sa 18:22. The courtiers were to talk to David בּלּט, “<hi type="italic">in private</hi>,” i.e., as though they were doing it behind the king’s back.
entries.a469b3d563fb737f253efe961738de27f1076986: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">1Sa 18:23</reference> <div eID="gen3981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3982" type="x-p"/> David replied to the courtiers, “<hi type="italic">Does it seem to you a little thing to become son-in-law to the king, seeing that I am a poor and humble man?</hi>” “<hi type="italic">Poor</hi>,” i.e., utterly unable to offer anything like a suitable dowry to the king. This reply was given by David in perfect sincerity, since he could not possibly suppose that the king would give him his daughter without a considerable marriage portion.
entries.813ae965aa69705e484b2f2be117c567855e5d92: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.24-1Sam.18.25">1Sa 18:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen3982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3983" type="x-p"/> When this answer was reported to the king, he sent word through his courtiers what the price was for which he would give him his daughter. He required no dowry (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.34.12">Gen 34:12</reference>), but only a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, i.e., the slaughter of a hundred Philistines, and the proof that this had been done, to avenge himself upon the enemies of the king; whereas, as the writer observes, Saul supposed that he should thus cause David to fall, i.e., bring about his death by the hand of the Philistines.
entries.1274cf42abdf57c48e1971d3d415bc98189bfddd: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26-1Sam.18.27">1Sa 18:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen3983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3984" type="x-p"/> But David was satisfied with Saul’s demand, since he had no suspicion of his craftiness, and loved Michal. Even before the days were full, i.e., before the time appointed for the delivery of the dowry and for the marriage had arrived, he rose up with his men, smote two hundred Philistines, and brought their foreskins, which were placed in their full number before the king; whereupon Saul was obliged to give him Michal his daughter to wife. The words “<hi type="italic">and the days were not full</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.26">1Sa 18:26</reference>) form a circumstantial clause, which is to be connected with the following sentence, “<hi type="italic">David arose</hi>,” etc. David delivered twice the price demanded. “<hi type="italic">They made them full to the king</hi>,” i.e., they placed them in their full number before him.
entries.8c511b762780ddd72c2fe5d8db44a188898565c8: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.28-1Sam.18.29">1Sa 18:28-29</reference> <div eID="gen3984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3985" type="x-p"/> The knowledge of the fact that David had carried out all his enterprises with success had already filled the melancholy king with fear. But when the failure of this new plan for devoting David to certain death had forced the conviction upon him that Jehovah was with David, and that he was miraculously protected by Him; and when, in addition to this, there was the love of his daughter Michal to David; his fear of David grew into a lifelong enmity. Thus his evil spirit urged him ever forward to greater and greater hardness of heart.
entries.2157ea293020419aad1c4bc5ce3ab17b2115b983: <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.30">1Sa 18:30</reference> <div eID="gen3985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3986" type="x-p"/> The occasion for the practical manifestation of this enmity was the success of David in all his engagements with the Philistines. As often as the princes of the Philistines went out (sc., to war with Israel), David acted more wisely and prosperously than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was held in great honour. With this general remark the way is prepared for the further history of Saul’s conduct towards David.  <chapter eID="1Sam.18"/> <div eID="gen3986" type="x-p"/>
